newsitem.title: USA: Balanced budget a question, despite deal - experts.
newsitem.headline: Balanced budget a question, despite deal - experts.

text.p: Have President Clinton and Congress finally found the way to the elusive balanced budget, or is their landmark deal to wipe out the deficit in five years just a lot of smoke and mirrors?
Budget experts -- while praising the deal for its bipartisan foundation, its spending cuts and its deficit reductions -- said a balanced budget by the year 2002 is still far from a sure thing.
"If the budget is balanced in 2002, it will be as much by luck as by design," said Stanley Collender, chief budget analyst with Burson-Marsteller.
"This has to be viewed with some scepticism," said Robert Reischauer, former congressional budget director, who questioned the economic assumptions used in coming up with the deal.

"It's a package that's based on expectations that the economic performance of the past five years will continue, and it would be very surprising if we went through the next five years without some contractions or sluggish growth."

Clinton and Republican leaders in Congress hammered out a historic five-year plan on Friday that cuts $115 billion from planned growth in the Medicare health care programme for the elderly, takes another $16 billion from the Medicaid programme for the poor, offers net tax cuts of $85 billion for the rich and the middle-class and promises a balanced budget by 2002.

Not since 1969 -- the year of the Woodstock rock festival, the year the underdog New York baseball team, the "Amazing Mets," won the World Series and the first year of Richard Nixon's presidency -- has the U.S. budget been balanced.

Clinton on Saturday said a balanced budget may be reached even sooner than 2002 if a projected windfall of $225 billion in extra tax revenues materialises. He was referring to a last minute revision from the Congressional Budget Office that upped tax revenues over the next five years by $225 billion because of the strong economy.
The unexpected revisions, released on Thursday night, saved budget negotiators from imposing more painful cuts.
But some experts said the rosy CBO numbers just enabled lawmakers and the White House to avoid making tough, needed decisions that will pave the way for needed reform after 2002.
"The real question is what have we done to make things after 2002 better, and the answer is virtually nothing," said Reischauer.

"This is a missed opportunity ... We had a window of opportunity to begin to make structural reforms in entitlement programmes so that we can make the changes that will be required in the years ahead."
Reischauer and other experts predicted big problems after 2002, when retiring baby boomers begin to dip into expensive government programmes such as Social Security and Medicare.
"The real challenge before the nation is the problem that will develop as baby boomers start to retire," he said.
But other fiscal experts were more sanguine.
"The federal budget is only supposed to be five years down the road -- it's not designed to take care of problems 10 years in the future," said Collender of Burson-Marsteller.
And besides, many observers said, Congress can always come back and change the budget before five years.
"I look at this as a one or a two-year deal," said Collender. "Anything longer approaches science fiction."
